title: Closing the Loop: Universal Repository Representation with RPG-Encoder
one_liner: Encode a code repository into one shared planning graph so that an agent can navigate, localize, and reconstruct the project from the same representation.
lead: Repository agents often work with fragmented views of a codebase. One tool may use API text, another may use file dependencies, and another may use retrieved snippets. That split makes it harder to reason across structure and meaning at the same time. RPG-Encoder proposes a single repository planning graph that is built from raw code and then updated incrementally, so that understanding and generation both rely on the same project representation.

problem.h2: Why repository agents lose the thread
paras: A software repository contains many connected facts: file roles, call relations, data flow, naming conventions, and higher-level intent. When an agent only sees one slice at a time, it may find the wrong file or misunderstand how several files work together.

This problem shows up in code localization and code generation. To localize a bug, the agent must compress a large codebase into the small set of relevant places. To generate code, it must expand a requested intent into changes that fit the existing project. The paper argues that these two tasks should share one project representation.

callout.b: The paper's move in one sentence.
callout.html: Build one repository planning graph from raw code, update it incrementally as the repository changes, and use that graph as the shared interface for understanding and generation.

steps.b: Read raw code into a planning graph
steps.text: Convert files and their relations into a repository planning graph that combines code meaning with structural links.
Connect functions, files, and modules so that the graph can expose cross-file context during navigation.
Evolve the graph incrementally because rebuilding the whole graph after every edit would cost too much on large repositories.
Query the graph to find the small set of likely relevant code locations.

steps.b: Use the same graph for reconstruction
steps.text: Generate or rebuild repository structure from the graph so that understanding and generation close the loop.

paras: The paper changes the basic representation that a repository agent relies on. Instead of switching between several partial views, the agent gets one graph that supports both reading the repository and writing back into it.
object.object: the repository representation used by the agent

hidden.name: the project-level intent that ties many code fragments together
paras: The key hidden quantity is the repository intent that is spread across files. A single file may show local logic, but the reason that logic exists often depends on neighboring files, call paths, and project conventions.

RPG-Encoder tries to recover that hidden project intent in one structure. The shared graph helps because it preserves structural links and meaning together, so a navigation step can use both kinds of evidence instead of guessing from text alone.

heat.caption: Darker cells mark the project-level facts that are hard to recover from isolated snippets but easier to recover from a shared graph.

reads.html: The hidden quantity is the larger project meaning that connects many small code pieces.
The method uses a unified repository planning graph to preserve enough project structure that understanding and generation can be treated as two directions through the same representation.

mechanism.h2: Why this works: one map is better than several partial maps
paras: Repository tasks fail when the agent has to stitch together unrelated views on the fly. A text-only view misses structural relations, while a relation-only view misses code meaning. RPG-Encoder keeps both in one graph so that a localization or generation step can read a richer neighborhood.

The incremental update rule also matters because a unified representation would be too costly if it had to be rebuilt from scratch after every change. The paper reports low maintenance overhead by updating only the affected region, which keeps the shared graph usable on large repositories.

stages.s: Encode them into one planning graph
Use the graph for localization and generation
A repository agent with a more coherent project view because both tasks share one representation

math.h2: Balance repository fidelity against maintenance cost
math.words: A compact summary is to value a repository representation when it preserves enough project detail for downstream tasks while keeping update cost low after edits.
symbols: overall value of the repository representation
how well the graph preserves useful project information
how much work is needed to keep the graph current after changes

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Graph A preserves strong project detail but needs a full rebuild after each edit.
Its fidelity is 9 and its update cost is 6, so with eta = 1 its total score is 3.
Graph B preserves almost as much detail and updates only local regions.
Its fidelity is 8 and its update cost is 1, so its total score is 7.
A system prefers Graph B because it remains informative without becoming too expensive to maintain.

math.note: The paper contains a richer implementation, but this equation captures the design tradeoff that the representation must stay both faithful and maintainable.

charts.title: Fragmented repository views
charts.note: Partial views miss project-level context, so localization and reconstruction both suffer while upkeep stays high.

charts.title: RPG-Encoder
charts.note: The paper reports stronger repository understanding because a shared graph keeps structure and meaning aligned while incremental updates reduce upkeep.

items.b: The graph may omit subtle code meaning.
items.html: If the encoding misses a critical project convention, the agent may trust the graph too much because the missing detail will not appear during navigation.
A local update rule may leave stale links behind if a change has wider effects than the updater notices.

items.b: Large graphs can become hard to query.
items.html: A unified representation can still slow down if the search procedure over the graph is weak, because too many candidate regions may look relevant.
The framework matters because it treats repository understanding and repository generation as two uses of the same project map.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a repository navigation demo on a medium-sized open-source project. Compare a baseline agent that retrieves files by text and dependency lists against an RPG-Encoder-style agent that queries a shared repository planning graph. Test both on bug localization and on small code-generation tasks that must fit project structure.

The demo should report top-k localization accuracy, reconstruction coverage for selected modules, and cost of keeping the representation current after controlled repository edits. The graph-based agent should win because one shared map lets it move between local code details and project-level structure more reliably.
demo.metric_eq: repo_gain = localization_score_rpg - localization_score_baseline ; upkeep_drop = update_cost_baseline - update_cost_rpg
demo.closing: The goal is to show that one repository representation can support both reading and writing the codebase.
